capabilities.statement: Explain why academic work acknowledges its sources

evidence.title: Community of practice note on why sources are acknowledged
evidence.example: You write a short explanation of why academic work names its sources, using Lave and Wenger's (1991) idea of legitimate peripheral participation: newcomers join a community of practice by taking part in its customs, and acknowledging sources is one of those customs. You link this to trust and to letting readers trace ideas (for example, why a history essay on the 1832 Reform Act credits the historians whose arguments it builds on).
evidence.artefact: A one-page explanatory note, with tutor comments, linking the acknowledgement of sources to joining an academic community of practice.
grounding: ing:doc:situated-learning-lave-wenger-1991

evidence.title: Tracing the sources behind a community leaflet
evidence.example: You take a real document from a part-time job or volunteering role and find where its figures and claims come from (for example, a food bank leaflet quoting NHS portion guidance). You then explain to your supervisor why naming that evidence matters to the people who read it, showing you understand that acknowledging sources is about accountability and trust, not only marks.
evidence.artefact: The annotated leaflet marking each claim and its source, with a short note on why acknowledgement matters to its readers.
grounding: professional: Explains why a report or piece of advice names the evidence it rests on and where it comes from.
professional: ICAI Fundamental Values (2021): honesty, trust

genericOutcomes.title: Linking source acknowledgement to joining a knowledge community
genericOutcomes.example: You write a short explanation of why serious written work names its sources, using the idea that newcomers join any community of practice by taking part in its shared customs. Acknowledging sources is one such custom: it signals honesty about where an idea came from and lets a reader trace it back to the original argument it builds on. You treat this as a mark of trust between writer and reader, not a formality that exists only to avoid being penalised.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A one-page note linking source acknowledgement to joining a knowledge community, with written feedback.
grounding: ing:doc:situated-learning-lave-wenger-1991

genericOutcomes.title: Tracing the sourced claims in a public-facing document
genericOutcomes.example: You take a real document written for a general audience and trace where its figures and claims come from, checking each one against its original source. You then explain, in a short note, why naming that evidence matters to the people who rely on the document, showing that acknowledging sources is about accountability and trust rather than something done only to earn a mark.
genericOutcomes.artefact: An annotated document marking each claim and its source, with a short note on why acknowledgement matters to readers.
grounding: professional: Explains why a report or piece of advice names the evidence it rests on and where it comes from.
professional: ICAI Fundamental Values (2021): honesty, trust

genericOutcomes.title: Explaining why selected sources must be named
genericOutcomes.example: Working from a short set of possible sources, you select the ones most relevant to a question and explain why naming them matters rather than simply listing them at the end. You set out how acknowledging where information comes from lets a reader judge the quality of what you selected and trace a claim back to its origin. You treat this naming as part of showing your selection was deliberate, not an afterthought added once the writing was finished.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short written explanation linking selected sources to the reasons they were chosen and named.
grounding: ing:doc:situated-learning-lave-wenger-1991
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/information-and-sources

genericOutcomes.title: Justifying chosen sources to an uninvolved colleague
genericOutcomes.example: You are asked to justify why you relied on particular sources of information when completing a piece of work. You explain, to someone who was not involved, which sources you selected, why they were appropriate to the task, and why you named them openly rather than presenting their conclusions as your own. This shows that selecting and acknowledging sources appropriate to the work is part of how you earn a reader's trust.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short written justification of the sources selected and acknowledged, reviewed by a colleague.
grounding: professional: Explains why a report or piece of advice names the evidence it rests on and where it comes from.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/information-and-sources

capabilities.statement: Construct accurate in-text references and a references list in one style

evidence.title: Annotated references list showing what each element does
evidence.example: You build the in-text citations and references list for a first assignment in your department's required style, then annotate three entries to explain how each element (author, date, title, publisher, page) helps a reader find the source. Drawing on Lave and Wenger (1991), you note that learning these conventions is part of moving from the edge of your subject community towards fuller participation (for example, Harvard author-date in a business studies report).
evidence.artefact: An annotated references list and matching in-text citations from an assignment, checked against the style guide, with margin notes.
grounding: ing:doc:situated-learning-lave-wenger-1991

evidence.title: Footnoted campaign briefing in an organisation's house style
evidence.example: You attribute sources in a document written for a real reader, following that organisation's house style rather than a module handbook (for example, a students' union campaign briefing where the officer asks for footnoted links to council data). You keep the style consistent and check that every citation leads to its source, showing you can construct accurate references when someone else sets the format.
evidence.artefact: The submitted briefing with its source notes, plus the house style guidance you followed and your checking notes.
grounding: professional: Attributes sources in reports, proposals and published material in the style the organisation or field requires.
professional: SCONUL Seven Pillars: Manage (recall: cites sources in suitable styles)

genericOutcomes.title: Annotating a references list to show what each element does
genericOutcomes.example: You build the in-text citations and references list for a short piece of work in one required style, then annotate three entries to explain how each element, such as author, date, title and publisher, helps a reader find the source. Drawing on the idea that learning these conventions is part of moving from the edge of a knowledge community towards fuller participation, you treat accuracy here as more than a formatting rule to satisfy.
genericOutcomes.artefact: An annotated references list and matching in-text citations, checked against a style guide, with margin notes.
grounding: ing:doc:situated-learning-lave-wenger-1991

genericOutcomes.title: Matching a required house style for sourced claims
genericOutcomes.example: You attribute sources in a document written for a real reader, following a required house style rather than a familiar set of conventions you already know well. You keep the style consistent throughout and check that every citation leads back to its source, showing that you can construct accurate references when someone else has set the format rather than when you chose it yourself.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A submitted document with its source notes, the house style guidance followed, and checking notes.
grounding: professional: Attributes sources in reports, proposals and published material in the style the organisation or field requires.
professional: SCONUL Seven Pillars: Manage (recall: cites sources in suitable styles)

genericOutcomes.title: Converting a mixed source list into one consistent style
genericOutcomes.example: Given a short list of sources found during research, you select the details each one needs, such as author, date, title and publisher, and convert every entry into one consistent citation style. You check each in-text citation against its matching reference so a reader could trace every claim back to where it was found. This demonstrates using sources appropriate to the task accurately and consistently, not only locating them.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A worked references list converted into one consistent style, checked against its in-text citations.
grounding: ing:doc:situated-learning-lave-wenger-1991
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/information-and-sources

genericOutcomes.title: Standardising citations across a shared piece of work
genericOutcomes.example: You are handed a draft containing citations in several inconsistent formats and asked to bring it into line with one required style before it goes out. You check each source is still correctly identified, correct any missing details, and make every citation and reference entry consistent. This shows that you can find, select and use sources accurately even when you did not collect them yourself.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A corrected draft with every citation standardised, plus a short note listing the changes made.
grounding: professional: Attributes sources in reports, proposals and published material in the style the organisation or field requires.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/information-and-sources

capabilities.statement: Record and organise sources as they are found, so every citation can be traced

evidence.title: Source log mapped to the SCONUL Manage pillar
evidence.example: You set up a source log for a project and map your routine to the Manage pillar of the SCONUL Seven Pillars of Information Literacy (SCONUL 2011), which covers organising information and citing it properly. You record full details, page numbers and access dates as you read, not afterwards, so every later citation can be traced (for example, a psychology lab report drawing on twelve journal articles).
evidence.artefact: A source log or reference manager library export, with a short commentary mapping your recording routine to the Manage pillar.
grounding: model: SCONUL Seven Pillars of Information Literacy (SCONUL 2011)

evidence.title: Placement evidence log behind a component specification
evidence.example: On a placement or in a job, you keep a record of where every figure in a piece of work came from, so a colleague could check it (for example, an engineering placement where you log the standards and supplier datasheets behind a component specification). You organise the record so items can be found quickly, showing the same traceability habit that referencing needs.
evidence.artefact: An evidence log or shared-drive index from the placement, with a supervisor's note confirming it was used to check figures.
grounding: professional: Keeps a record of the sources and evidence used, so that any figure or claim can be traced.
professional: Concordat to Support Research Integrity: accountability

genericOutcomes.title: Mapping a source log to an information literacy model
genericOutcomes.example: You set up a log for every source you plan to use in a piece of work and map your routine to a recognised information literacy model, which treats organising and citing information as a distinct skill rather than an afterthought. You record full details, page numbers and the date you accessed each source as you read, not afterwards, so that every citation you later write can be traced back to where it came from.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A source log or reference manager export, with a short commentary mapping the routine to the model.
grounding: model: SCONUL Seven Pillars of Information Literacy (SCONUL 2011)

genericOutcomes.title: Keeping a traceable record of evidence behind a piece of work
genericOutcomes.example: In a role where you produce work others will check, you keep a record of where every figure or claim came from, organised so a colleague could find it quickly. You log sources as you use them rather than reconstructing the list afterwards, showing the same traceability habit that accurate referencing depends on, and you can point to a specific figure and its source on request.
genericOutcomes.artefact: An evidence log or index from the work, with a note confirming it was used to check figures.
grounding: professional: Keeps a record of the sources and evidence used, so that any figure or claim can be traced.
professional: Concordat to Support Research Integrity: accountability

genericOutcomes.title: Logging sources at the point of selection, not afterwards
genericOutcomes.example: As you find and select sources for a piece of work, you record each one immediately, noting enough detail that it could be traced and used again later. You organise the log so related sources sit together, rather than treating recording as a step to complete once the writing is finished. This shows that selecting sources appropriate to a task includes keeping a usable record of the selection itself.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A source log built during research, organised by theme, with full details recorded at point of selection.
grounding: model: SCONUL Seven Pillars of Information Literacy (SCONUL 2011)
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/information-and-sources

genericOutcomes.title: Building a traceable record while gathering evidence
genericOutcomes.example: While gathering evidence for a task, you keep a running record of where each source came from and how it was used, organised well enough that a colleague could pick it up without asking you. You treat this record as part of selecting sources properly, not as paperwork added once the real work is done. This shows that finding and using sources appropriate to a task includes keeping them traceable throughout.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A running evidence record built during the task, reviewed by a colleague for completeness.
grounding: professional: Keeps a record of the sources and evidence used, so that any figure or claim can be traced.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/information-and-sources

capabilities.statement: Acknowledge quotation and paraphrase correctly, avoiding plagiarism

evidence.title: Patchwriting check and revision of a drafted paragraph
evidence.example: You compare a paragraph you drafted from a source with the original, using Howard's (1995) idea of patchwriting, where a writer stays too close to the source's wording and sentence structure. You mark any patchwritten phrases, then either quote them with quotation marks and a page number or rewrite them as a genuine paraphrase with a citation (for example, a law student summarising a Supreme Court judgment).
evidence.artefact: Side-by-side drafts: the source, your first attempt with patchwritten phrases marked, and the revised version with correct quotation and attribution.
grounding: model: Patchwriting (Howard 1995)

evidence.title: Ward newsletter summary with quotation and paraphrase marked
evidence.example: You report someone else's words and findings accurately in a real setting, marking what is quoted and putting the rest in your own words with credit (for example, a nursing student writing a ward newsletter item that summarises a new NICE guideline). You decide when an exact quotation is needed and when a paraphrase serves the reader better, and you credit both.
evidence.artefact: The newsletter item, with the source attached and the quoted and paraphrased passages highlighted for comparison.
grounding: professional: Reports others' words and findings accurately, marking what is quoted and putting the rest in own words with attribution.
professional: ICAI Fundamental Values (2021): honesty

genericOutcomes.title: Checking a draft paragraph for patchwriting
genericOutcomes.example: You compare a paragraph you drafted from a source with the original wording, checking for patchwriting, where a writer stays too close to the source's sentence structure while changing only a few words. You mark any patchwritten phrases, then either quote them properly with quotation marks and a page reference or rewrite them as a genuine paraphrase with a citation, so the final version reflects your own understanding of the material.
genericOutcomes.artefact: Side-by-side drafts: the source, the first attempt with patchwritten phrases marked, and the corrected version.
grounding: model: Patchwriting (Howard 1995)

genericOutcomes.title: Marking quotation and paraphrase in a shared summary
genericOutcomes.example: You report someone else's words and findings accurately in a short item written for other people, marking clearly what is quoted and putting the rest in your own words with credit. You decide, claim by claim, when an exact quotation best serves the reader and when a paraphrase does, and you credit the original source either way, so nothing in the summary could be mistaken for your own finding.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A written summary with the source attached and the quoted and paraphrased passages highlighted.
grounding: professional: Reports others' words and findings accurately, marking what is quoted and putting the rest in own words with attribution.
professional: ICAI Fundamental Values (2021): honesty

genericOutcomes.title: Demonstrating subject knowledge through accurate paraphrase
genericOutcomes.example: Given a passage central to a topic, you paraphrase it in your own words and compare your version against the original to check no distinctive phrasing has survived unmarked. Where your understanding is incomplete, the paraphrase tends to drift back towards the source's wording, so you treat that drift as a signal to reread the passage rather than patch the sentence. This links accurate paraphrase to genuinely understanding the subject's core content, not just rearranging words.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A paraphrased passage with the original attached and notes on where understanding was checked.
grounding: model: Patchwriting (Howard 1995)
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/subject-knowledge-and-understanding

genericOutcomes.title: Showing understanding by paraphrasing a technical passage for others
genericOutcomes.example: You are asked to explain a technical passage to someone without specialist background, in your own words, while being honest about which parts are a close paraphrase and which are a direct quotation worth keeping intact. Doing this well depends on genuinely understanding the core content, since a shaky grasp shows up as wording that drifts back towards the original. You credit the source either way, showing both your understanding and your honesty.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A written explanation for a general reader, with the source credited and quoted passages marked.
grounding: professional: Reports others' words and findings accurately, marking what is quoted and putting the rest in own words with attribution.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/subject-knowledge-and-understanding

evidence.title: Core elements breakdown of awkward source types
evidence.example: You reference awkward sources, such as a translated novel, a chapter in an edited book, a dataset and a social media post, by working through the core elements template in the MLA Handbook (Modern Language Association 2021): author, title, container, other contributors, version, number, publisher, date and location. You then convert each entry into your required style, showing you understand what each element does (for example, in a modern languages essay).
evidence.artefact: A worked table breaking each tricky source into its core elements, with the final reference in your required style.
grounding: model: MLA core elements template (Modern Language Association 2021)

evidence.title: Credits page and decision note for a live design brief
evidence.example: On a live brief or society project, you credit sources that do not fit a standard pattern (for example, a design student crediting a client's brand guidelines, a licensed stock image, a podcast interview and an online exhibition). You check the style guide or ask a librarian, record each decision, and apply it consistently, showing you can handle unfamiliar source types accurately.
evidence.artefact: The project's credits or references page, plus a decision note recording how each unusual source type was referenced and why.
grounding: practice: live design brief for an external client

genericOutcomes.title: Breaking an unfamiliar source into its core elements
genericOutcomes.example: You reference an awkward source, such as a translated work, a chapter inside an edited collection, a dataset or an online post, by working through a core elements template covering author, title, container, other contributors, version, number, publisher, date and location. You then convert the entry into a required citation style, checking that every element that exists for that source type has been captured correctly rather than guessed at.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A worked table breaking an unusual source into its core elements, with the final reference in a required style.
grounding: model: MLA core elements template (Modern Language Association 2021)

genericOutcomes.title: Recording how an unusual source was credited
genericOutcomes.example: On a project where sources do not fit a standard pattern, such as a set of guidelines, a licensed image, an interview recording or an online exhibit, you credit each one, checking a style guide or asking someone with more experience when the format is unclear. You record each decision so it can be repeated consistently, showing that you can handle unfamiliar source types accurately rather than skipping or guessing at them.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A project credits page plus a decision note recording how each unusual source type was referenced.
grounding: framework: SCONUL Seven Pillars: Manage (recall: cites sources in suitable styles)

genericOutcomes.title: Selecting the right template for an awkward source type
genericOutcomes.example: Given a source that does not fit the usual pattern, such as a dataset, a translated text or a piece of software, you work out which elements a reader would need to find it again, rather than forcing it into a template built for a book or an article. You select and record only the details that genuinely identify that source, showing that using sources appropriate to the task includes adapting how you cite the ones that do not fit easily.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short worked reference for an awkward source type, with notes on the elements selected and why.
grounding: model: MLA core elements template (Modern Language Association 2021)
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/information-and-sources

genericOutcomes.title: Referencing an unfamiliar source type under time pressure
genericOutcomes.example: You are given a source you have not had to cite before, such as a recorded interview, a dataset or an exhibition, and asked to reference it correctly before a deadline. You check the available guidance, select the elements that identify that source, and record your decision so a colleague could follow the same approach next time. This shows that finding and using sources appropriate to the task extends to ones that are unfamiliar.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A completed reference for an unfamiliar source type, with a short note on the decision made.
grounding: framework: SCONUL Seven Pillars: Manage (recall: cites sources in suitable styles)
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/information-and-sources

capabilities.statement: Use citation to show the scope of research and engagement with the discourse

evidence.title: Citation map showing which conversations your essay joins
evidence.example: You analyse the references list of your own essay and sort the citations into strands: foundational works, recent studies, opposing views and primary sources. Using Lave and Wenger's (1991) community of practice idea, you explain what your citations tell a reader about which conversations in the field you have joined, and add sources where a strand is missing (for example, a sociology essay on gig work that cited only one side).
evidence.artefact: A citation map of your essay's references grouped by strand, with a revision note on the gaps you filled before submission.
grounding: ing:doc:situated-learning-lave-wenger-1991

evidence.title: Evidence-backed recommendation for a sports club
evidence.example: You prepare a recommendation for a real decision and show the range and quality of the evidence behind it (for example, a sport science student on placement at a rugby club advising on hamstring injury prevention, citing systematic reviews, a governing body guideline and the club's own injury data). You explain to the reader why that evidence base is enough for the decision, and where it is thin.
evidence.artefact: The recommendation paper with its evidence summary table, and the coach's feedback on whether it informed the decision.
grounding: professional: Shows the range and quality of the evidence behind a recommendation.
professional: ICAI Fundamental Values (2021): trust

genericOutcomes.title: Mapping a reference list into strands of engagement
genericOutcomes.example: You analyse your own reference list and sort the citations into strands, such as foundational works, recent studies, opposing views and primary sources. Drawing on the idea that joining a knowledge community means engaging with its different conversations, you read what your citations tell a reader about which of those conversations you have joined, and you add sources where a strand is thin or missing before finishing the work.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A citation map of a reference list grouped by strand, with a note on gaps filled before submission.
grounding: ing:doc:situated-learning-lave-wenger-1991

genericOutcomes.title: Showing the evidence base behind a real recommendation
genericOutcomes.example: You prepare a recommendation for a genuine decision and set out the range and quality of the evidence behind it, distinguishing strong, directly relevant sources from weaker or more tangential ones. You explain to the reader why that evidence base is enough to support the decision, and where it remains thin, so your citations do more than list what you happened to read.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A recommendation with an evidence summary table and feedback on whether it informed the decision.
grounding: professional: Shows the range and quality of the evidence behind a recommendation.
professional: ICAI Fundamental Values (2021): trust

genericOutcomes.title: Showing research scope through a reference list's range
genericOutcomes.example: You review a piece of your own writing and ask what its reference list reveals about the scope of your research, rather than only whether each citation is correctly formatted. You check whether the sources span enough of the relevant conversation, including views that disagree with your own, and treat gaps in that range as a sign your research was narrower than the sources appropriate to the task required.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short review of a reference list's range, noting where coverage was too narrow and how it was widened.
grounding: ing:doc:situated-learning-lave-wenger-1991
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/information-and-sources

genericOutcomes.title: Demonstrating research scope through cited evidence
genericOutcomes.example: Before presenting a recommendation, you check that the sources you have gathered show the genuine scope of your research, not just the first few that supported your initial view. You deliberately seek out sources appropriate to the task that challenge your position, and you cite them alongside the supporting evidence, so a reader can see the breadth of what you considered before reaching a judgement.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A citation list for a recommendation showing both supporting and challenging sources considered.
grounding: professional: Shows the range and quality of the evidence behind a recommendation.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/information-and-sources

capabilities.statement: Uphold honesty and trust in academic work

evidence.title: Case analysis of an honesty decision in your own work
evidence.example: You write a case analysis of one integrity decision in your own work, using the ICAI Fundamental Values of Academic Integrity (ICAI 2021), which name honesty, trust, fairness, respect, responsibility and courage. You focus on honesty and trust: what you did when a result was weaker than expected or a source could not be checked, and how your choice protected the reader's ability to rely on your work (for example, a chemistry lab report with an anomalous result).
evidence.artefact: A case analysis of one integrity decision, with the relevant extract from your submitted work, linked to honesty and trust.
grounding: model: ICAI Fundamental Values of Academic Integrity (ICAI 2021)

evidence.title: Correcting an overstated figure during an internship
evidence.example: In a workplace or project, you report work honestly when it would be easier not to (for example, a computing student on a summer internship telling the team that test coverage figures in a release note were overstated, and correcting them). You record what you reported and why, showing you understand that colleagues and clients need to be able to rely on what you say.
evidence.artefact: The corrected record or message to the team, with a short note from your line manager confirming what happened.
grounding: professional: Reports work, results and sources honestly so that colleagues and clients can rely on them.
professional: Concordat to Support Research Integrity: honesty, transparency and open communication

genericOutcomes.title: Analysing one honesty decision against a values framework
genericOutcomes.example: You write a short case analysis of one integrity decision in your own work, using a framework that names honesty, trust, fairness, respect, responsibility and courage as fundamental values. You focus on honesty and trust: what you did when a result was weaker than expected or a source could not be verified, and how that choice protected a reader's ability to rely on your work afterwards.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A case analysis of one integrity decision, with the relevant extract, linked to honesty and trust.
grounding: model: ICAI Fundamental Values of Academic Integrity (ICAI 2021)

genericOutcomes.title: Correcting an overstated figure before it was relied on
genericOutcomes.example: In a piece of work, you report something honestly when it would have been easier not to, such as telling a team that a figure in a shared document was overstated and correcting it before anyone relied on it. You record what you reported and why, showing that you understand colleagues and clients need to be able to trust what you tell them, even when the honest answer is inconvenient to deliver.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A corrected record or message, with a short note confirming what happened and when.
grounding: professional: Reports work, results and sources honestly so that colleagues and clients can rely on them.
professional: Concordat to Support Research Integrity: honesty, transparency and open communication

genericOutcomes.title: Weighing an ethical issue raised by a weak result
genericOutcomes.example: Faced with a result that is weaker or messier than expected, you set out the ethical issue it raises: whether to present it as stronger than it is, to quietly drop it, or to report it honestly with its limitations explained. You reason through each option against the responsibility to let a reader trust what you report, and you justify the choice you make rather than simply following the easiest path available.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short reasoned note setting out the ethical issue raised by a weak result and the choice made.
grounding: model: ICAI Fundamental Values of Academic Integrity (ICAI 2021)
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/ethics

genericOutcomes.title: Acting on an ethical responsibility to report accurately
genericOutcomes.example: You notice that a figure or claim in a piece of shared work is not well supported, and you recognise this as an ethical responsibility rather than a minor detail to let pass. You raise it, explain why it matters, and help correct the record, even though staying quiet would have been easier and probably gone unnoticed. This shows acting on an ethical responsibility rather than only recognising that one exists.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A record of the issue raised, the correction made, and confirmation from someone else involved.
grounding: professional: Reports work, results and sources honestly so that colleagues and clients can rely on them.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/ethics

capabilities.statement: Uphold fairness, respect, responsibility and courage in academic conduct

evidence.title: Group project conduct analysed against four integrity values
evidence.example: You analyse a group project against four ICAI (2021) values: fairness, respect, responsibility and courage. You set out how credit was shared, how you responded to others' ideas, what you owned when things went wrong, and whether you raised a concern you could have ignored (for example, an architecture studio group where one member's drawings were presented without credit). You judge where your conduct met each value and where it fell short.
evidence.artefact: A structured analysis of your group project conduct against the four values, with evidence such as meeting notes or contribution records.
grounding: model: ICAI Fundamental Values of Academic Integrity (ICAI 2021)

evidence.title: Raising a concern about an uncredited shared resource
evidence.example: In a society role, placement or job, you take responsibility for fair treatment of other people's work and raise a concern when something is wrong (for example, as a course representative in education studies, you tell staff that a revision guide is being shared without its author's permission, and help agree a fair fix). You record the steps you took and how you treated the people involved with respect.
evidence.artefact: A dated record of the concern raised, the response and the outcome, with confirmation from a staff member or society officer.
grounding: professional: Treats colleagues' work fairly and with respect, takes responsibility for own work and raises concerns when something is wrong.
professional: ICAI Fundamental Values (2021): fairness, respect, responsibility, courage

genericOutcomes.title: Analysing group conduct against four integrity values
genericOutcomes.example: You analyse a group project against four values named in an integrity framework: fairness, respect, responsibility and courage. You set out how credit for ideas was shared, how you responded when someone else's work was presented without full credit, what you owned when something went wrong, and whether you raised a concern you could have let pass, judging where your conduct met each value and where it fell short.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A structured analysis of group conduct against four values, with evidence such as meeting notes.
grounding: model: ICAI Fundamental Values of Academic Integrity (ICAI 2021)

genericOutcomes.title: Raising a concern about an uncredited shared resource
genericOutcomes.example: In a group or team setting, you take responsibility for the fair treatment of other people's work and raise a concern when something is wrong, such as noticing that a shared resource is being used without its creator's permission. You help agree a fair fix, and you record the steps taken and how you treated the people involved with respect throughout, rather than letting the issue drop because raising it felt uncomfortable.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A dated record of the concern raised, the response and the outcome, with confirmation from someone involved.
grounding: professional: Treats colleagues' work fairly and with respect, takes responsibility for own work and raises concerns when something is wrong.
professional: ICAI Fundamental Values (2021): fairness, respect, responsibility, courage

genericOutcomes.title: Reasoning through a fairness issue in shared work
genericOutcomes.example: You identify a fairness issue in a piece of shared work, such as one contributor's input going unacknowledged, and reason through what fairness, respect and responsibility require of you as the person who noticed it. You weigh the discomfort of raising the issue against the responsibility to act, and set out the course of action that courage requires, even where staying silent would be the easier choice.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short reasoned note analysing a fairness issue against the values of respect, responsibility and courage.
grounding: model: ICAI Fundamental Values of Academic Integrity (ICAI 2021)
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/ethics

genericOutcomes.title: Acting with courage to correct an unfair outcome
genericOutcomes.example: You notice that someone's contribution to shared work has gone unacknowledged, and you recognise this as an ethical responsibility rather than someone else's problem to solve. You raise the issue with the people involved, treating them with respect even where the conversation is uncomfortable, and you help put in place a fairer outcome. This shows acting on an ethical responsibility for fairness rather than only noticing that one exists.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A record of the fairness issue raised, the response from those involved, and the outcome agreed.
grounding: professional: Treats colleagues' work fairly and with respect, takes responsibility for own work and raises concerns when something is wrong.
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/ethics

capabilities.statement: Carry integrity into graduate and professional identity

evidence.title: Professional identity statement linking integrity to a code
evidence.example: You write a professional identity statement that links your record of academic integrity to the code of conduct of the profession you are entering, drawing on Wenger's (1998) account of communities of practice, in which learning shapes identity as well as knowledge. You identify which habits carry across, which change, and what the profession will expect of you (for example, a postgraduate pharmacy student mapping referencing and data honesty to the GPhC standards for pharmacy professionals).
evidence.artefact: A professional identity statement mapping your integrity practices to a named professional code, suitable for a portfolio or interview.
grounding: model: Communities of practice (Wenger 1998)

evidence.title: Source-checking routine set up for a policy team
evidence.example: You carry an integrity commitment into a setting where you hold real responsibility (for example, a master's student in social research on a policy internship who sets up a source-checking and attribution routine for the team's briefings, then trains a new intern in it). You show that integrity is now part of how you work as a professional, not only how you meet assessment rules.
evidence.artefact: The routine or protocol you wrote, examples of its use in briefings, and a reference or note from your supervisor.
grounding: practice: postgraduate policy internship

genericOutcomes.title: Mapping personal integrity habits onto a professional code
genericOutcomes.example: You write a short statement linking your own record of academic integrity to the code of conduct of a profession you intend to enter, drawing on the idea that learning within a community shapes identity as well as knowledge. You identify which of your current habits, such as careful attribution and honest reporting, carry across into that code, which will need to change, and what the profession will expect of you that your current habits do not yet cover.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A professional identity statement mapping integrity practices onto a named professional code.
grounding: model: Communities of practice (Wenger 1998)

genericOutcomes.title: Setting up an integrity routine for a team you join
genericOutcomes.example: In a setting where you hold real responsibility for the first time, you set up a source-checking and attribution routine for the team's work, then teach it to someone newer than you. You treat this as carrying your integrity commitment into how you work as a professional, not only as something that applied to assessed work, and you can point to the routine being used by someone other than yourself.
genericOutcomes.artefact: The written routine, examples of its use, and a note confirming someone else adopted it.
grounding: framework: ICAI Fundamental Values (2021): honesty, trust
framework: Concordat to Support Research Integrity: accountability

genericOutcomes.title: Recognising which ethical habits carry into a profession
genericOutcomes.example: You examine your own habits around honesty, attribution and care for other people's work, and ask which of these count as ethical responsibilities that a profession will also expect of you, rather than rules that applied only to assessed coursework. You identify where the expectations will tighten, such as higher stakes for a dishonest claim, and where your existing habits already meet what the role will require of you.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short written comparison of personal ethical habits against the expectations of a named professional role.
grounding: model: Communities of practice (Wenger 1998)
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/ethics

genericOutcomes.title: Carrying an ethical responsibility into a new professional role
genericOutcomes.example: Starting in a role where your work affects other people for the first time, you recognise an ethical responsibility you previously only met for assessment purposes, such as checking claims before passing them on, and you act on it without being asked. You explain the habit to someone newer than you, showing that the responsibility has become part of how you work rather than a rule you follow only when checked.
genericOutcomes.artefact: A short account of the ethical habit carried into the new role, with a note from someone who observed it.
grounding: framework: ICAI Fundamental Values (2021): honesty, trust
benchmark: qaa-universal/threshold/ethics
